newsitem.title: USA: CEO leaves Ben & Jerry's after two years on job.
newsitem.headline: CEO leaves Ben & Jerry's after two years on job.

text.p: Ben & Jerry's Homemade Inc., the iconoclastic ice cream maker known for its quirky product names and corporate largess, said Friday that Robert Holland was resigning as president and chief executive after less than two years in the job.
The company's stock lost $1, or almost 8 percent, immediately after the news was announced, but the shares recovered to trade at $12.625, down 62.5 cents, in midday trading on the Nasdaq market.
Ben & Jerry's said earlier this month that it expected its third-quarter earnings to be "materially' below last year's.

Holland replaced the firm's famous founders early in 1995, when the company -- originally known for its counter-culture corporate culture -- moved from a "founder-led" system to a more professional management structure.

As health-conscious Americans began swearing off fattening foods, Holland was brought in to introduce the company's products, like "Cherry Garcia" and "Chunky Monkey" ice cream, to sweet-toothed consumers overseas.

"Bob arrived just when we needed him to help straighten out our operations, get our new plant up and running, start our international business and launch our new sorbet line. We are very grateful for his contribution," co-founder and Chairman Ben Cohen said in a brief statement announcing Holland's sudden departure, effective Oct. 31.

Holland was hired after the company launched an unorthodox executive search campaign through newspaper advertisements in which it invited would-be candidates to write essays explaining why they were suited for the job. After receiving more than 22,500 responses to its "Yo, I'm Your CEO" write-in campaign, Ben & Jerry's announced that it had hired Holland, although there were reports that he was actually found through an executive search firm.

The no-nonsense, button-downed executive -- the antithesis of the bearded, tie-dyed founders of the company, whose scruffy visages appear on every pint -- did manage to restore order to Ben & Jerry's operations and finances. But he may have lost a struggle over the company's direction.

Holland argued that Ben & Jerry's must expand more aggressively. Cohen, who with Jerry Greenfield turned a correspondence course in ice cream-making into a $150 million company, favored slower growth that would not harm the socially-conscious company's relations with its employees or the tiny Vermont communities where it operates.

Ben & Jerry's pledges 7.5 percent of its pretax profits to social causes -- from antinuclear campaigns to gay rights. It also uses its purchasing power to back its values, buying milk and cream from Vermont family farms, even though it costs more.
The company also gives three free pints of ice cream a day to each of its 700 employees, most of whom wear jeans or shorts to work.
"Ben & Jerry's has great products, great people and a promising future," Holland said in a statement.

"However, at this juncture a change appears appropriate. When you couple the marketplace challenges with the predictably tough demands associated with succeeding founders, the need for accelerated succession is clear."

The company, however, does not have a successor for Holland, who had vowed to make the unorthodox manufacturer and retailer more profitable by tighter management of areas such as raw materials, distribution, inventories and waste.
The announcement said a subcommittee of the board would begin a serach for a new CEO.
The company said Holland, a former chief executive of a plastics firm and consultant to Fortune 500 companies, will remain as a director through June 1997.
Bruce Bowman, senior director of operations, was given the additional title of chief operating officer on an interim basis and would oversee day-to-day management of the company, it said.
